body:
We make Kiron, and our founding team used Fitbod nearly every day for about seven years before building it. Fitbod's prices and features here come from its help center and App Store listing, checked November 15, 2026, plus an independent guide to its export file. Everything about Kiron describes version 1.2.

If you're looking for a Fitbod alternative, it's probably the price, or the feeling that the app decides everything without telling you why. We know that second one well. Here's how Kiron (that's us) compares, and when Fitbod is still the right pick.

Fitbod or Kiron? The quick verdict

  • Choose Kiron if you want to open the app and just train, for about half the price: {{kiron:price-annual}}, against Fitbod's $95.99. Kiron runs a ready-made program for your goal, or the plan you already have, and raises your weights as you get stronger.
  • Stay with Fitbod if you want a brand-new workout every session with no plan at all, you train with an Apple Watch or Wear OS watch, or you rely on its exercise videos.
  • Switching is easy: Kiron imports your Fitbod history.

Bottom line: both apps spare you the planning. Fitbod makes up each workout; Kiron follows a program and adjusts it. For most people, we think the program is the better deal: it costs less, you chose it, and you can see where it's headed.

What Kiron is

Kiron is a workout app for {{kiron:cell-platforms}} that runs a training program for you. Start in one of three ways:

  • Pick one of {{kiron:program-count}} ready-made programs for your goal (samples below).
  • Answer a few questions and Kiron builds one.
  • Bring your own plan. Paste it from ChatGPT, a coach or a website, or snap a photo, and Kiron turns it into a program on your calendar.

Then there's little to think about:

  • Your next workout is ready when you open the app, whether you train on set days or whenever you make it to the gym.
  • Your weights go up as you get stronger, and Kiron tells you why: "You hit every set, so we added 5 lb."
  • Variety that keeps your main lifts. Smaller exercises can rotate week to week; the big lifts stay put, so you can watch them climb.
  • Ready for travel. Save a hotel or second gym with its equipment, and switching to it swaps in exercises that fit.
  • Runs and races on the same calendar as your lifting, with plans from a first 5K to a marathon or a sprint triathlon.
  • {{kiron:offline-lead}} {{kiron:offline-detail}}
  • About half Fitbod's yearly price: {{kiron:price-annual}}, against $95.99.

A sample of the {{kiron:program-count}} programs

  • Strength: Beginner 5×5, Novice Linear Progression, Wave Loading Strength, Upper / Lower Strength
  • Muscle: Push / Pull / Legs, Five-Day Split, Full Body Muscle, Glute Builder
  • New to training: First Month in the Gym, Bodyweight Beginner
  • Home or little equipment: Dumbbell Full Body, Kettlebell Strength, Resistance Band Full Body
  • Running: Beginner 5K, Run a 10K, Half Marathon, Marathon
  • Hybrid and races: Run + Lift, Sprint Triathlon, Fitness Race Prep, Cycling Base
  • Joint-friendly: Strong Knees, Healthy Back

Many follow formats lifters and runners have used for decades, like a 5×5 or a push/pull/legs split, so you start with a proven structure, not a blank page.

Two ways to not think about your workouts

Fitbod's selling point is that you don't have to plan: open it, and it builds a workout from your history, equipment and which muscles have recovered. Kiron keeps that promise differently: a ready-made program does the planning, and Kiron adjusts the weights as you go.

This part is our founding team's experience, not a lab result.

What Fitbod gets right

Credit where it's due. Fitbod is good at handing you a fresh workout with no plan at all, and it's a polished app. Its exercise videos and how-tos are very good; most of Kiron's exercises have an animated demo instead.

Both apps rotate exercises for variety, save more than one gym for travel, add warm-up sets, shorten a workout when you're pressed for time, and count other apps' workouts (through Apple Health or Health Connect) toward muscle recovery.

What frustrated us, and what Kiron does instead

  • Not knowing why. Fitbod picks some exercises and skips others, and we often couldn't tell why. Beyond more, less or never for an exercise, and each gym's equipment, we couldn't steer it, and changing things by hand defeated the point of it learning what we wanted. In Kiron, your plan is on the calendar, and when Kiron adds weight, it tells you why. If muscles are still tired from other workouts, it names them and offers an easier session.
  • Starting weights that were way off. Back on an exercise after a while, the suggestion could be far too easy: say, 15 lb per arm on another curl when you curl 100 lb on a curl bar. Kiron starts from what you last lifted, a little lighter after time away, and counts history you import from Fitbod. New to an exercise? It works from a related lift you've logged, so a 100 lb curl-bar curl sets your dumbbell curls, and a short note says why. After your first set it asks how the weight felt and adjusts the rest.
  • The exercises we wanted every leg day. Fitbod's My Plan can keep one focus lift per training day, but we couldn't make sure our own handful showed up every leg day. In Kiron, your program decides what's on leg day, and its main lifts don't change. If smaller exercises rotate, "Keep this every week" holds one in place and "Don't mix this in again" drops one.
  • Working around an injury. We couldn't tell Fitbod to stop working a muscle while an injury healed; setting a muscle's recovery by hand isn't a pause. Kiron handles this one exercise at a time: rest an exercise, or swap it out, for a few weeks or months, and it comes back on its own.
  • Making room for core work. We couldn't get Fitbod to fit a core or lower-back routine into the week where it made sense. In Kiron, "Add to today" adds core work to any workout in a few taps, with arms, shoulders, glutes, calves, a cardio finisher and stretching on the same menu.

That's the trade: Fitbod decides fresh each time; Kiron decides once, with a program you chose, then handles the weights, variety, travel and tired muscles.

Fitbod's prices are the ones its help center lists for new subscribers; earlier subscribers may still pay the older $12.99 and $79.99 its App Store listing shows. A lifetime membership appears only as an occasional promotion. Prices vary by country and offer.

On the yearly plans, Kiron costs about half what Fitbod does. Paying monthly, it's {{kiron:price-monthly}}, against Fitbod's $15.99. Both give new subscribers 7 days free.

Switching from Fitbod, history and all

  1. Export from Fitbod. In its Settings, tap Export Workout Data. It saves your logged workouts as a spreadsheet file (CSV).
  2. Start Kiron. Pick a program or paste your plan, and choose your training days.
  3. Bring your history. In Kiron's Settings, tap Import from another app and choose the Fitbod file. Kiron shows how it matched each exercise before saving, and you can remove an import later.
  4. Train. For exercises in your Fitbod history, Kiron starts from your last numbers. For anything new, it suggests a starting weight, says why, and asks after your first set how it felt.
  5. Cancel Fitbod where you subscribed, before it renews.

Kiron has no export of its own, so hold on to that Fitbod file. Our guide to exporting your workout history covers other apps too.

Who should stay with Fitbod

  • You want a brand-new workout every session, with no plan at all. That's what Fitbod is built for.
  • You train with a watch. Fitbod has Apple Watch and Wear OS apps; Kiron has neither, and reads heart rate from Apple Health or Health Connect afterwards.
  • Videos matter to you. Fitbod's exercise videos and how-tos are very good, where most of Kiron's exercises have an animated demo.
  • You value a long track record. Fitbod has about 290,000 ratings on the US App Store, averaging 4.8. Kiron is new and still small.

Quick answers about Fitbod

Is Fitbod free, and did its price go up?

No. There's no free plan: new users get 7 days free, then pay $15.99 a month or $95.99 a year, per Fitbod's help center. That's up from the $12.99 and $79.99 its App Store listing still shows, which earlier subscribers may still pay.

Is there an app like Fitbod but cheaper, or free?

Kiron is {{kiron:price-monthly}} or {{kiron:price-annual}}, and its ready-made programs do the planning in a different way. If you'd rather pay nothing, Hevy's free plan logs unlimited workouts with up to 4 saved routines (see Hevy vs Kiron), and Boostcamp offers most of its coach-made programs free. For workouts generated fresh each time, like Fitbod's, look at FitnessAI, Gravl or Planfit. Or see our guide to workout apps for following a program.

Can I take my Fitbod history with me?

Yes. In Fitbod's Settings, Export Workout Data saves your logged workouts as a file that Kiron can import; the steps are above.

Is Fitbod worth it for beginners?

It can be, if you want an app to make every choice while you learn; the videos help, and 7 free days is enough to judge its picks. The other way in is a beginner program with the same main lifts each week, so you learn them and watch your numbers climb, like Kiron's First Month in the Gym or Beginner 5×5.

If Fitbod's price, or not knowing why it picks what it picks, brought you here, try Kiron. Pick a program for your goal or paste the plan you follow, bring your Fitbod history, and your week is laid out for you. {{kiron:cta-sentence}} Get Kiron.

If Fitbod's picks suit you and the price doesn't bother you, staying put is a good answer.
